title: Topper Headon - Wikipedia
notes: Nicholas Bowen Headon, born 30 May 1955, Bromley, Kent; grew up in Crockenhill, Dover Grammar School for Boys; nicknamed for Mickey the Monkey in the Topper comic. A soul and jazz fan who cites Billy Cobham as a strong influence (citing Greg Prato's AllMusic biography). Mirkwood, a progressive rock band, from 1973 for about a year and a half (supporting Supertramp); a band that supported the Temptations. A week with London SS. Joined the Clash in 1977 meaning to make a name and move on, stayed four and a half years; first show 26 April 1977, Rouen. Drums on Give 'Em Enough Rope, the US The Clash, London Calling, Sandinista! and Combat Rock; sang 'Ivan Meets G.I. Joe'. Composed most of the music of 'Rock the Casbah' and played its drums, piano and bass. Left on 10 May 1982 at the start of the Combat Rock tour, over heroin; Strummer: 'How can I be singing anti-drug songs with you sitting behind me?' Drumming style: 'a simple bass-snare up-down beat with closed hi-hat flourishes' (Clash City Rockers, Clampdown, Train in Vain, Lost in the Supermarket); Train in Vain 'one of the most important and distinctive beats in rock music' (Scott Kenemore, PopMatters, 2007); Sandy Pearlman called him 'The Human Drum Machine' for his timing and skill (Prato). After the Clash: Samurai, the solo album Waking Up (1986), a cover of Gene Krupa's 'Drumming Man' (1985); Carbon/Silicon with Mick Jones, 2008; Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the Clash, 2003.

title: Will Brewster, 'Gear Rundown: London Calling by The Clash', Mixdown, 20 May 2025
notes: Quotes Headon's interview with Mike Dolbear: 'When I joined The Clash I had a silver Premier kit that I brought up from Dover'; not wanting to take his own kit on the road, at Henrit's on Wardour Street 'there was a big silver, mirror finish Pearl kit there', which he used for his whole time in the band; always Zildjian cymbals, 15-inch hats; 'Paiste I always found a bit light and thin.' Calls his style primarily jazz-influenced, with a tendency to 'swing his eighth notes', yet heavy enough for Strummer and Simonon.

title: Paul Matts, ''Topper' Headon: An Appreciation', We Are Cult, 10 April 2019
notes: Self-taught, his technique 'learnt from watching drummers, Buddy Rich, Keith Moon'; his hero Billy Cobham; jazz, rock, funk, soul and blues. On joining: 'I thought, I'm going to have to knock the shit out of those drums. As a result, I had to re-learn my style.' Pearlman: 'a human drum machine'. Song by song: Tommy Gun's machine-gun snare; Jimmy Jazz 'a laid-back jazz pattern'; Wrong 'Em Boyo fluid ska; Train in Vain a loop-style smack copied on many later drum machine tracks; The Magnificent Seven funk; Should I Stay or Should I Go power rock 'yet slightly funky'; Rock the Casbah written while waiting for the band.

title: Jon Wurster, 'Encore: Topper Headon on the Clash's London Calling', Modern Drummer, 23 September 2011
notes: Headon let the band 'actually execute such disparate styles' (reggae, ska, rockabilly, Motown); Clampdown the 'barnstorming rocker', Train in Vain 'R&B-flavored', Revolution Rock 'ska-infused'; 'one of the best and most versatile rock drummers of all time'. Bill Price's engineering credited for the record's sound.

title: Reuben Cross, 'Topper Headon: the hidden "genius" in The Clash', Far Out, 15 May 2026
notes: Strummer on Rock the Casbah: 'He banged down the drum track, then ran over to the piano and then the bass'; 'The real genius of "Rock The Casbah" is Topper.' Terry Chimes, his predecessor, took his place for the Combat Rock tour and appeared in the video.

title: ''Topper' Headon, My Story', Dover Express, 19 August 2004 (reproduced by the Old Pharosians)
notes: His first press interview in twenty years: 'anointed Topper by the band' in 1977; Terry Chimes, 'drummer from the first album', took his place; he busked on the Underground on the bongos. 'I loved playing live, touring and life on the road.'

title: Complete Control - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded at Sarm East Studios, Whitechapel, July 1977, produced by Lee 'Scratch' Perry, engineered by Mickey Foote; 'Topper Headon's first recording with the band, following the departure of Terry Chimes'. UK No. 28, the band's first top 30.

title: (White Man) In Hammersmith Palais - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded at Basing Street, London, March-April 1978, produced by Sandy Pearlman and the Clash, engineered by Simon Humphries; released 16 June 1978 (CBS 6383). Topper Headon, drums. Mick Jones: 'a mixture of the reggae influence and punk'; a guitar intro, then a slower ska rhythm. UK No. 32.

title: Give 'Em Enough Rope - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded March-April and August-September 1978 at Basing Street (London) and the Automatt (San Francisco), produced by Sandy Pearlman, engineered by Corky Stasiak; Pearlman 'ensured the drums were mixed louder than Strummer's vocals on the entire album'. Q: 'their drumming problems were over with the arrival of jazz-trained [Topper] Headon'. Safe European Home opens side one.

title: London Calling - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 149,285. Rehearsed at Vanilla Studios, Pimlico, mid-1979 (the Vanilla Tapes); recorded at Wessex Studios from August 1979 in five or six weeks of 18-hour days; produced by Guy Stevens, engineered by Bill Price. The band came to recognise 'drummer Topper Headon's skills', usable in many genres beyond punk. Punk, new wave, ska punk, reggae, rockabilly, New Orleans R&B, lounge jazz and hard rock. Clampdown began as the instrumental 'Working and Waiting'; The Guns of Brixton is Simonon's first lead vocal.

title: Train in Vain - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded at Wessex, 1979, Guy Stevens; Topper Headon drums and percussion. Written for an NME flexi disc, then added to London Calling after the sleeve was printed (Bill Price: 'the last song we finished'), so unlisted. Mick Jones: 'The track was like a train rhythm.' Butch Vig 'used a drum loop from "Train in Vain"' for Garbage's 'Stupid Girl' (1995). US No. 23.

title: Combat Rock - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 102,452. Recorded 1980, September 1981, November 1981 to January 1982 and April 1982 at Ear (London), Electric Lady (New York) and Warnham (Glyn Johns's home studio); produced by the Clash and Glyn Johns, who mixed it. Headon wrote the music of Rock the Casbah and recorded its drums, piano and bass; 'Topper Headon was fired (due to his heroin addiction) days before the release of Combat Rock', replaced by Terry Chimes, 'whom Headon had replaced in 1977'. No per-track drummer is listed beyond Rock the Casbah.

title: Rock the Casbah - Wikipedia
notes: Headon composed the music 'based on a piano part that he had been toying with'; alone in the studio he 'progressively taped the drum, piano and bass parts'; the others found the instrumental 'essentially complete'. Released 11 June 1982; US No. 8, 'their only top 10 single in that country'; the single is a Mick Jones and Bob Clearmountain remix.

title: Should I Stay or Should I Go - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded 1981, produced by the Clash; Mick Jones lead vocal, Strummer and Joe Ely the Spanish backing vocals; credited to Headon, Jones, Simonon and Strummer. UK No. 17 (1982); UK No. 1 on its 1991 reissue, the band's only one. No drummer named and no description of the drums.
